ODU_208_Òtúá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity (c. 11th–14th Century CE): Codified at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as Òtúá-Túúrúpọ̀n, governing sacred prayers sanctifying difficult child deliveries, maternal survival, and neonatal blessings. 19th-Century Era: Consulted in maternity sanctuaries across Egba and Oyo territories during wartime evacuations. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí Ifá as Otura Trupon, invoked for pediatric prayers and motherly strength.
ODU_208_Òtúá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Òtúá (I/II/I/I: prayer, illumination, divine release) on the right and Òtúúrúpọ̀n (II/II/I/II: maternal nurture, carrying life) on the left of Ọpọ́n Ifá. Dialectically balances celestial prayers with the earthly burden of childbirth, teaching that sincere spiritual petitions convert physical labor into triumphant life.
ODU_208_Òtúá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn on Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/II/I/I on the right and II/II/I/II on the left. The Babaláwo strikes the eastern quadrant with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Ọ̀já-Ọmọ, Ewé Tètè, cold water, pure shea butter, and a white hen.
ODU_208_Òtúá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for expectant mothers experiencing prolonged labor, families consecrating newborns, and pediatric prayer vigils.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òtúá gbàdúrà, Òtúúrúpọ̀n bí ọmọ rẹ̀ láyọ̀; àdúrà tí a fi ìrẹ̀lẹ̀ gbà kì í kùnà. (Òtúá prayed, and Òtúúrúpọ̀n delivered her infant in triumph; the prayer offered with humility never fails: Fervent faith turns perilous labor into joyful arrival.)

Ẹrù tí abiyamọ ń rù kì í fọ́ ọmọ; agbára Ọlọ́run ló ń gbé wa ró. (The load carried by a devoted mother never crushes the infant; divine strength is what sustains us: Maternal sacrifices are crowned by divine grace.)
ODU_208_Òtúá_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

ODU_209_Òtúá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Òtúá-Rẹtẹ̀ or Òtúá-Tẹtẹ́, governing surgical recovery, pharmacological herbal baths, and trampling stubborn pestilence. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by herbal medicine battalions treating wounded soldiers. Contemporary/Diaspora: Preserved in Lucumí as Otura Rete, celebrating therapeutic cleansing and disease excision.
ODU_209_Òtúá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Òtúá (prayer, release) and Ìrẹtẹ̀ (trampling down disease, surgical incision, purification). Demonstrates that spiritual supplication and rigorous botanical science must cooperate; praying without taking medicine is folly, just as medicine without spiritual alignment lacks enduring vigor.
ODU_209_Òtúá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá with Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/II/I/I on the right and I/I/II/I on the left. The Babaláwo touches the southern perimeter with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Ìrẹtẹ̀, Ewé Ṣaworo, sulfur-and-chalk bath, and consecrated palm oil.
ODU_209_Òtúá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.social_and_ritual_context: Divined for chronic patients facing long-term physical illness, individuals recovering from surgeries, and communal epidemiological cleansings.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òtúá ké sí ọ̀run, Ìrẹtẹ̀ tẹ àrùn mọ́lẹ̀; àpapọ̀ àdúrà àti egbògi ló ń wo aláìsàn sàn. (Òtúá called upon heaven, and Ìrẹtẹ̀ trampled disease underfoot; the synthesis of prayer and medicinal roots cures the afflicted: Spiritual devotion combined with active healing restores wholeness.)

Bí a kò bá wẹ ara nù, a kì í rí àyè fún ìbùkún; ìmọ́tótó ni aṣọ ìlera. (Unless one washes away bodily impurities, one finds no space for blessings; cleanliness is the vestment of health: Rigorous hygiene ensures longevity.)
ODU_209_Òtúá_Ìrẹtẹ̀.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_210_Òtúá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Òtúá-Ṣẹ́, the sacred convergence of answered prayer and Ọ̀ṣun's riverine sweetness, celebrated for lifting severe depression and economic stagnation. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by female guild leaders dedicating trading ships along Osun and Ogun waterways. Contemporary/Diaspora: Maintained in Lucumí as Otura She, celebrated for sweetening bitter destinies.
ODU_210_Òtúá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Òtúá (prayer, light) and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (sweetness, beauty, Ọ̀ṣun's victory). Teaches that the ultimate validation of prayer is not stern severity, but the flowering of human sweetness, fertility, and communal celebration.
ODU_210_Òtúá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/II/I/I on right and I/II/I/II on left. The Babaláwo sprinkles consecrated river water across Ọpọ́n Ifá. Prepared with pure honey, Ewé Ọ̀ṣun, yellow sulfur chalk, bronze bell, and sixteen cowries.
ODU_210_Òtúá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for artists, merchants, and individuals emerging from bitter grief seeking emotional rejuvenation and matrimonial harmony.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òtúá gbàdúrà, Ọ̀ṣẹ́ da oyin sí i; ẹni tí ó ba gba ìmọ́lẹ̀ yóò rí adùn ayé. (Òtúá offered prayer, and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ poured honey upon it; he who receives divine light shall taste life's sweetness: Pure devotion dissolves bitterness.)
Oyin kì í korò láéláé; ọkàn tí ó mọ́ kì í gbé inú ìbànújẹ́ pẹ́. (Honey is never bitter; the pure heart never abides in sorrow for long: Divine sweetness overcomes sorrow.)
ODU_210_Òtúá_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_211_Òtúá_Òfún.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Òtúá-Fún, the supreme coronation of the Òtúá cycle, uniting prayer with Ọbàtálá's pristine white mantle of creation. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by the high council of Ọbàtálá priests in Ilé-Ifẹ̀ during peace assemblies. Contemporary/Diaspora: Maintained in Lucumí as Otura Fun, crowning prayers with divine legitimacy and immaculate clarity.
ODU_211_Òtúá_Òfún.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Òtúá (prayer, illumination) and Òfún (primordial purity, creation, supreme white clay). Teaches that when sincere prayer ascends to the primordial source, all corruption is washed white; ethical purity is the highest form of spiritual power.
ODU_211_Òtúá_Òfún.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá with Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/II/I/I on right and II/I/II/I on left. The Babaláwo sweeps Ìyẹ̀rosùn with a white Ìrùkẹ̀rẹ̀ whisk and draws a ring of Ẹfun. Involves pure white chalk (Ẹfun), Ewé Òdúndún, cold water, sixteen land snails, and white linen.
ODU_211_Òtúá_Òfún.social_and_ritual_context: Divined for high-ranking spiritual leaders, royal coronation purifications, and sealing long-standing community reconciliations.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òtúá ké sí Ọ̀run, Òfún fi aṣọ funfun wọ̀ ọ́; ẹni tí ó bá wọ aṣọ ìmọ́lẹ̀ kì í tẹ́. (Òtúá called upon Heaven, and Òfún clothed it in white vestments; he who wears the garment of divine light is never disgraced: Absolute moral integrity guarantees triumph.)

Ẹfun funfun kì í ba aṣọ jẹ́; ìwà tútù ló ń gbé oríire ga. (Pristine chalk never corrupts the cloth; a serene and gentle character elevates good fortune: Gentle righteousness commands universal honor.)
ODU_211_Òtúá_Òfún.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_212_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ogbè.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity (c. 11th–14th Century CE): Codified at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Ogbè, also revered as Ẹrọ-Ìrẹtẹ̀, the paramount sovereign chapter of physical revitalization, conquering debilitating weakness, and clearing paths for lasting prosperity. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by warrior kings to rejuvenate weary armies after protracted campaigns. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Irete Untelu / Irete Ogbè, renowned for overcoming physical collapse.
ODU_212_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ogbè.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (I/I/II/I: trampling down disease, carving, firm footstep) on the right and Ogbè (I/I/I/I: primordial light, total victory) on the left of Ọpọ́n Ifá. Dialectically represents decisive surgical mastery illuminated by cosmic consciousness, teaching that debilitating obstacles must be actively dismantled with clear vision.
ODU_212_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ogbè.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn across Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/I/II/I on the right and I/I/I/I on the left. The Babaláwo strikes the central hearth (`Àárín Ọpọ́n`) with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Ìrẹtẹ̀, Ewé Tètè, pure palm oil, honey, rooster to Ògún, and white pigeon to Orí.
ODU_212_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ogbè.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for individuals suffering prolonged physical exhaustion, business leaders reviving collapsed ventures, and communities clearing sacred roads.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ tẹ ibi mọ́lẹ̀, Ogbè gbé ire ró; ẹni tí ó ba nífẹ̀ẹ́ sí àlàáfíà gbọ́dọ̀ múra sí iṣẹ́. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ trampled evil underfoot, and Ogbè erected righteousness; he who desires peace must apply himself to industrious labor: Decisive action backed by divine light ensures prosperity.)

Ọ̀nà tí ó kún fún ẹ̀gún kì í dènà ẹni tí ó wọ bàtà; ìfaradà ló ń bẹ́ agbára lórí. (A path laden with thorns cannot halt the one who wears sturdy shoes; patient fortitude subdues adversity: Preparedness overcomes life's hazards.)
ODU_212_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ogbè.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_213_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Yẹ̀kú, governing strict epidemiological quarantines, stamping out ancestral curses of premature mortality, and subduing nocturnal pestilence. 19th-Century Era: Invoked during smallpox outbreaks to isolate infected quarters and protect healers. Contemporary/Diaspora: Preserved in Lucumí as Irete Yeku, invoking Ọbalúayé for disease pacification.
ODU_213_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (trampling down disease, medicinal excision) and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (darkness, mortality, cooling, ancestral twilight). Teaches that the threat of death is neutralized through courageous confrontation and meticulous hygiene; retreating in panic spreads contagion.
ODU_213_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/I/II/I on right and II/II/II/II on left. The Babaláwo taps the southern edge with a consecrated horn Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Ìran, Ewé Akòko, black earthenware vessel, cold spring water, and shea butter.
ODU_213_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.social_and_ritual_context: Divined during severe communal contagions, chronic family illnesses, and averting impending generational fatalities.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ tẹ ikú mọ́lẹ̀, Ọ̀yẹ̀kú paná àrùn; ẹni tí ó gbọ́n kì í bá àìsàn ṣeré. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ trampled death underfoot, and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú quenched the fire of disease; the prudent initiate never trifles with sickness: Vigorous medical intervention preserves life.)

Bí a bá pẹ́ nínú òkùnkùn, ojú ń mọ́lẹ̀ díẹ̀díẹ̀; sùúrù ló ń sọ àìlera di agbára. (When one stays in darkness, sight gradually adjusts; patient endurance transforms debility into strength: Resilience outlasts dark hours.)
ODU_213_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_214_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìwòrì.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Wòrì, governing diagnostic vision in traditional medicine, uncovering hidden pathologies, and discerning psychosomatic roots of illness. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by master herbalists diagnosing obscure ailments in royal courts. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Irete Yero, celebrated for diagnostic and analytical mastery.
ODU_214_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìwòrì.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (carving, healing action) and Ìwòrì (visionary inquiry, deep contemplation). Emphasizes that medical treatment without diagnostic perception is dangerous guesswork; the true physician must understand the spiritual and mental roots of physical infirmity.
ODU_214_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìwòrì.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/I/II/I on right and II/I/I/II on left. The Babaláwo strokes Ọpọ́n with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́ while chanting diagnostic verses. Involves Ewé Gbégbé, Ewé Àjídèwe, clear river water, honey, and a white dove.
ODU_214_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìwòrì.social_and_ritual_context: Cast when patients suffer mysterious ailments that defy conventional cures, and during apprentice inductions into herbalist guilds.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìwòrì wo ìsàlẹ̀ àrùn, Ìrẹtẹ̀ fi egbògi wo ó sàn; oníṣègùn tí kò gbọ́n ń ba oògùn jẹ́. (Ìwòrì looked beneath the affliction, and Ìrẹtẹ̀ healed it with medicinal roots; the healer who lacks insight wastes medicine: Accurate diagnosis is the root of recovery.)

Ojú tí ó mọ́ ló ń rí ohun tí ó wà nínú igbó; ìmọ̀ jinlẹ̀ ló ń gba ẹ̀mí là. (Clear eyes perceive what lies hidden in the forest; profound knowledge is what delivers human life: Deep understanding overcomes confusion.)
ODU_214_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìwòrì.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_215_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òdí.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Dí, governing physical convalescence, sealing bodily wounds against infection, and fortifying domestic health perimeters. 19th-Century Era: Consulted after battle victories to heal soldiers and purify city gates. Contemporary/Diaspora: Maintained in Lucumí as Irete Di, invoked for wound closure and domestic defense.
ODU_215_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òdí.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (healing incision, purification) and Òdí (rampart, closure, barrier). Demonstrates that once a wound or crisis is treated, the boundary must be firmly sealed; leaving the convalescent exposed to toxic elements invites fatal relapse.
ODU_215_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òdí.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/I/II/I on right and I/II/II/I on left. The Babaláwo seals the mark with a consecrated river stone. Involves Ewé Pèrègún, Ewé Tètè, smooth river stone, shea butter, and a rooster.
ODU_215_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òdí.social_and_ritual_context: Divined for post-surgical recovery, protecting homes against recurring infections, and sealing peace treaties.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ wo ọgbẹ́ sàn, Òdí ti ẹnu-ọ̀nà rẹ̀; ẹni tí ó ba san kì í tún padà sí ibùsùn àìsàn. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ healed the wound, and Òdí sealed its gateway; he who is cured must not return to the sickbed: Disciplined recovery prevents relapse.)

Odi tí a mọ dáradára kì í jẹ́ kí afẹ́fẹ́ ibi wọlé; ààbò ara ni baba ìwàláàyè. (A properly constructed rampart never permits noxious winds to enter; physical fortification sustains life: Vigilant boundaries preserve health.)
ODU_215_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òdí.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_216_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìrosùn.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Rosùn, governing hematological vitality, cleansing blood disorders, and restoring ancestral vigor through sacred camwood (Osùn). 19th-Century Era: Consulted by lineage elders when youth suffered chronic blood fevers. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Irete Lazo / Irete Iroso, celebrated for bloodline healing.
ODU_216_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìrosùn.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (cleansing incision, health) and Ìrosùn (ancestral blood, vigilance, camwood). Teaches that physical vitality is tied to the purity of the bloodline; honoring ancestral moral disciplines cleanses hereditary taints.
ODU_216_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìrosùn.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/I/II/I on right and I/I/II/II on left. The Babaláwo blends red camwood (Osùn) with Ìyẹ̀rosùn across Ọpọ́n Ifá. Involves Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, Osùn powder, white rooster, pure honey, and red parrot feather.
ODU_216_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìrosùn.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for patients suffering from anemia, circulatory ailments, or hereditary generational illnesses requiring ancestral cleansing.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ fọ ẹ̀jẹ̀ mọ́, Ìrosùn fi osùn kun ara; ẹ̀mí tí ó mọ́ kì í bẹ̀rù àìsàn. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ cleansed the bloodstream, and Ìrosùn anointed the body with camwood; the purified spirit fears no sickness: Clean bloodline vitality sustains robust life.)

Ọmọ tí ó gbé ẹ̀jẹ̀ àwọn baba rẹ̀ ga kì í tẹ́; orísun mímọ́ ló ń mú ìlera wá. (The child who upholds the ancestral bloodline never falters; a pure source produces radiant health: Ancestral alignment revitalizes life.)
ODU_216_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìrosùn.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art.

ODU_217_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Wọ́nrín, governing sudden medical emergencies, breaking stubborn fevers, and reversing chaotic physical decline. 19th-Century Era: Invoked during military marches when troops faced sudden pestilential exhaustion. Contemporary/Diaspora: Maintained in Lucumí as Irete Juani, invoked for breaking recurring domestic crises.
ODU_217_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (medicinal action, trampling disease) and Ọ̀wọ́nrín (sudden reversal, turbulent tempest). Demonstrates that severe physical and economic crises require bold, decisive intervention; hesitation amidst acute danger guarantees defeat.
ODU_217_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/I/II/I on right and II/II/I/I on left. The Babaláwo strikes the southwestern quadrant with an Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Iná, Ewé Èṣìṣì, palm kernel oil, roasted corn, and a spotted rooster.
ODU_217_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.social_and_ritual_context: Divined during acute domestic health crises, sudden financial downturns, and rapid escalation of disputes.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ tẹ egbò, Ọ̀wọ́nrín yi ìjì padà; nígbà tí ogun bá le, a kì í fi ìmọ̀ràn falẹ̀. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ stamped out the sore, and Ọ̀wọ́nrín turned back the tempest; when danger escalates, one must not delay action: Bold medicinal decisiveness triumphs over crisis.)

Ìjì líle kì í gbé ẹni tí ó ba mọ ibi tí ó ń lọ lọ; ìrètí rere ń borí àdánwò. (The tempest never sweeps away the traveler who knows their destination; steadfast hope overcomes severe trials: Purposeful fortitude conquers adversity.)
ODU_217_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_218_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀bàrà.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Bàrà, governing economic recovery after chronic illness, restoring market wealth, and warning against squandering health on vain luxury. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by merchant guild matrons recovering from seasonal illnesses. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Irete Bara, celebrated for turning medical recovery into commercial success.
ODU_218_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀bàrà.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (health, excision) and Ọ̀bàrà (abundance, nobility, modesty). Teaches that good health is the foundation of enduring wealth; restoring one's body without cultivating modest, ethical stewardship results in lost fortune.
ODU_218_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀bàrà.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/I/II/I on right and I/II/II/II on left. The Babaláwo taps the northern quadrant with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Ajé, Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, pure honey, sixteen cowries, and a white pigeon.
ODU_218_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀bàrà.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for entrepreneurs recovering from medical setbacks, individuals regaining livelihood, and business partnerships.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ wo ara sàn, Ọ̀bàrà gbé ọrọ̀ wọlé; ìlera ni ipìlẹ̀ gbogbo ọrọ̀ tí ń pẹ́. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ restored physical health, and Ọ̀bàrà ushered wealth into the home; good health is the bedrock of enduring prosperity: Vitality enables lasting accomplishment.)

Ọrọ̀ tí kò ní ìlera dàbí ilé tí a kọ́ sórí iyanrìn; ìtẹ́lọ́rùn ló ń gbé adé ga. (Wealth without health is like a house built upon sand; humble contentment elevates the crown: True wealth begins with wholeness.)
ODU_218_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀bàrà.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_219_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀kànràn.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Kànràn, governing the healing of psychosomatic afflictions caused by guilt, stern moral accountability, and dispelling slander. 19th-Century Era: Consulted in judicial tribunals when an accused person fell ill from moral distress. Contemporary/Diaspora: Maintained in Lucumí as Irete Kana, invoked for judicial vindication.
ODU_219_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀kànràn.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (healing incision, purification) and Ọ̀kànràn (thunder, stern conscience, direct speech). Teaches that hidden deceit poisons physical organs; sincere confession and moral restitution are necessary prerequisites for physical recovery.
ODU_219_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀kànràn.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/I/II/I on right and II/II/II/I on left. The Babaláwo strikes Ọpọ́n center with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Ọ́kìkà, Ewé Tètè, ram offering, shea butter, and cold spring water.
ODU_219_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀kànràn.social_and_ritual_context: Divined during bitter court trials, resolving internal moral torments, and treating patients whose illness stems from unconfessed wrongs.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ wo ara, Ọ̀kànràn sọ òtítọ́; ọkàn tí ó mọ́ kì í jẹ́ kí ara ṣe àárẹ̀. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ treated the physical frame, and Ọ̀kànràn proclaimed the truth; the conscience that is clean never permits the body to wither from guilt: Moral rectitude heals from within.)

Òtítọ́ korò ṣùgbọ́n ó ń wo aláìsàn sàn; ẹni tí ó ba jẹ́wọ́ yóò rí àánú gbà. (Truth may taste bitter yet it cures the patient; he who confesses his wrong shall find mercy: Honest confession brings profound relief.)
ODU_219_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀kànràn.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun: Old World and New; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination.

ODU_220_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ògúndá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Gúndá, the paramount chapter of surgical metallurgy, anatomical dissection, bone-setting, and surgical tool consecration. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by master surgeons and bone-setters across the Ekiti federation. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Irete Kutan / Irete Ogunda, celebrated for surgical safety and clearing obstacles.
ODU_220_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ògúndá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (incision, trampling sickness) and Ògúndá (iron blade, technological courage). Represents the sacred courage of the surgeon who wields iron not to kill, but to excise tumorous death and preserve life.
ODU_220_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ògúndá.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/I/II/I on right and I/I/I/II on left. The Babaláwo touches consecrated iron surgical implements to Ọpọ́n center. Involves Ewé Pèrègún, iron filings, roasted yam, palm oil, and a rooster to Ògún.
ODU_220_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ògúndá.social_and_ritual_context: Cast before complex surgical operations, setting compound bone fractures, dedicating surgical blades, and clearing dense virgin forests.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògún mú idà, Ìrẹtẹ̀ bẹ́ àrùn dànù; ọwọ́ oníṣẹ́-abẹ tí ó mọ̀fẹ́ kì í ṣìnà. (Ògún took up the blade, and Ìrẹtẹ̀ excised disease; the hand of the skilled surgeon guided by sacred wisdom never falters: Consecrated technical skill delivers life.)

Irin kì í pa ẹni tí ó bọ̀wọ̀ fún un; ọgbọ́n àti ìmọ̀ràn ló ń wo ọgbẹ́ sàn. (Iron never slays the one who reveres its sacred laws; wisdom and skilled counsel heal the deepest wound: Respect for metallurgy ensures safety.)
ODU_220_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ògúndá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Williams, Denis (1974). Icon and Image.

ODU_221_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀sá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Sá or Ìrẹtẹ̀-Ànsá, governing the healing of psychic disturbances, appeasing the nocturnal mothers (*Àwọn Ìyámi*), and dispelling spiritual fatigue. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by female elders in riverine areas during mysterious sleep fevers. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Irete Ansa, invoking Yemọja and nocturnal maternal spirits.
ODU_221_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀sá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (healing action, cleansing) and Ọ̀sá (flight, nocturnal spirits, astral wind). Teaches that physical ailments often have roots in strained relations with maternal and nocturnal forces; humility and ritual respect restore harmony between visible and invisible realms.
ODU_221_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀sá.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/I/II/I on right and II/I/I/I on left. The Babaláwo uses an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́ to circle the northern perimeter of Ọpọ́n. Involves Ewé Ègé, Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, cold maize gruel (Ẹ̀kọ), white pigeon, and cooked rabbit offering.
ODU_221_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀sá.social_and_ritual_context: Divined when patients experience chronic nightmares, unexplained psychic exhaustion, or require reconciliation with maternal lineage spirits.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀sá gbé afẹ́fẹ́ wá, Ìrẹtẹ̀ wẹ ara nù; ẹni tí ó ba bọ̀wọ̀ fún àwọn ìyá kì í rí ìpọ́njú. (Ọ̀sá brought the spirit wind, and Ìrẹtẹ̀ cleansed the body; he who reveres the nocturnal mothers encounters no affliction: Respect for maternal power unlocks immunity.)
Afẹ́fẹ́ tútù ló ń pa iná ìbínú; ìrẹ̀lẹ̀ ọkàn ń ra àlàáfíà wọlé. (The cooling breeze quenches the fire of wrath; humility of soul ushers serene peace indoors: Reconciliatory grace heals.)
ODU_221_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀sá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_222_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìká.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Ká, governing the extraction of biological poisons, neutralizing snake venom, and unraveling malicious conspiracies targeting healers. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by frontier scouts navigating venomous snake-infested forests. Contemporary/Diaspora: Preserved in Lucumí as Irete Ka, renowned for neutralising poison and traps.
ODU_222_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìká.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (carving, healing incision) and Ìká (restraint, the viper's coil, snare). Teaches that malicious traps and toxic poisons are defeated through vigilant medical knowledge and unyielding moral courage; panic allows venom to reach the heart.
ODU_222_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìká.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/I/II/I on right and II/I/II/II on left. The Babaláwo uses an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́ to cut a raffia thread on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Involves Ewé Ègé, Ewé Àlùpàyídà, antivenom charcoal infusions, white pigeon, and severed raffia cord.
ODU_222_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìká.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for patients suffering from poisoning, venomous snakebites, toxic litigation, and malicious traps set by competitors.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ yọ oró ejò dànù, ó ba àwọ̀n Ìká jẹ́; olóye kì í jẹ́ kí oró wọ inú ẹ̀jẹ̀ rẹ̀ lọ. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ extracted the serpent's venom and destroyed the net of Ìká; the wise person never allows venom to penetrate their bloodstream: Rapid antivenom mastery neutralizes malice.)

A kì í fi owó ibi mú ẹran tí ó ní oró; ẹni tí ó gbẹ́ kòtò ibi yóò kọsẹ̀ sí inú rẹ̀. (One does not handle venomous game with carelessness; he who constructs a malicious pit shall stumble into it: Treachery destroys its creator.)
ODU_222_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ìká.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.

ODU_223_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Túúrúpọ̀n or Ìrẹtẹ̀-Tutu, governing pediatric resilience, soothing infant fevers, and protecting pregnant mothers from seasonal epidemics. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by midwives treating displaced mothers during the Kiriji war. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Irete Tutu / Irete Trupon, celebrated for infant medicine.
ODU_223_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (healing action, purification) and Òtúúrúpọ̀n (maternal care, carrying life). Dialectically unites medicinal rigor with tender maternal compassion, teaching that children flourish when medicinal care is administered with gentle love.
ODU_223_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/I/II/I on right and II/II/I/II on left. The Babaláwo taps the southern edge with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Ọ̀já-Ọmọ, Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, cold maize gruel (Ẹ̀kọ), shea butter, and snail water.
ODU_223_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.social_and_ritual_context: Divined for sick infants, nursing mothers seeking pediatric protection, and dedicating family nurseries.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ wo ọmọ sàn, Òtúúrúpọ̀n pọ̀n ọn mọ́ra; ọwọ́ tútù ló ń tọ́ ọmọdé dàgbà. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ healed the infant, and Òtúúrúpọ̀n strapped the child to her back; gentle cooling hands nurture the child toward maturity: Loving compassion completes medicinal healing.)

Ẹrù ọmọ kì í wuwo lójú abiyamọ; sùúrù ni oògùn tí ó ń tọ́ iran iwájú. (The burden of an infant is never too heavy in the eyes of a true mother; patience is the medicine that rears the coming generation: Tender maternal devotion guarantees the future.)
ODU_223_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúúrúpọ̀n.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.

ODU_224_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúá.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Túá, governing the spiritual empowerment of pharmacology, uniting prayer with medicinal formulations, and spiritual covenants of non-violence. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by diplomatic emissaries offering medicinal relief to war-torn regions. Contemporary/Diaspora: Maintained in Lucumí as Irete Suka / Irete Otura, celebrated for prayers healing body and soul.
ODU_224_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúá.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (medicinal action, purification) and Òtúá (prayer, divine covenant, light). Demonstrates that spiritual faith without practical medicine is empty presumption, while medicine without divine blessing lacks life-giving aṣẹ; both must walk together.
ODU_224_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúá.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/I/II/I on right and I/II/I/I on left. The Babaláwo sweeps Ìyẹ̀rosùn with a white horse-tail whisk (Ìrùkẹ̀rẹ̀). Involves Ewé Ẹfun, Ewé Tètè, white chalk (Ẹfun), pure honey, and a white dove.
ODU_224_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúá.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during peace treaty ratifications, consecration of medical infirmaries, and prayer sessions for healing stubborn chronic ailments.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òtúá gbàdúrà, Ìrẹtẹ̀ bu oògùn fún aláìsàn; àdúrà tí a fi iṣẹ́ gbé lẹ́yìn ló ń mú àlàáfíà wá. (Òtúá prayed, and Ìrẹtẹ̀ administered medicine to the sick; prayer supported by practical labor brings enduring peace: Faith and medical craft operate in harmony.)

Àdúrà olódodo ń fún egbògi ní aṣẹ; ìmọ́lẹ̀ Ọlọ́run ló ń wo gbogbo àìsàn sàn. (The prayer of the righteous endows herbal roots with authority; the light of the Divine cures all infirmity: Spiritual alignment activates medicine.)
ODU_224_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òtúá.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Law, Robin (1977). The Oyo Empire.

ODU_225_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Ṣẹ́, governing the restoration of cosmetic beauty after illness, healing skin scarring, and Ọ̀ṣun's sweetening of convalescent waters. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by royal women regaining vitality after arduous postpartum recoveries. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Irete She, celebrating radiant health and sweetness.
ODU_225_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (healing, incision) and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (sweetness, beauty, Ọ̀ṣun's grace). Teaches that the end goal of physical healing is not merely the cessation of pain, but the full restoration of joy, radiant beauty, and creative vitality.
ODU_225_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/I/II/I on right and I/II/I/II on left. The Babaláwo sprinkles consecrated river water upon Ọpọ́n Ifá. Prepared with pure honey, Ewé Ọ̀ṣun, yellow chalk, bronze bells, and sweet bananas.
ODU_225_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.social_and_ritual_context: Divined for recovering patients seeking rejuvenation of beauty, matrimonial celebrations, and blessing natural water springs.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ bọ́ àrùn dànù, Ọ̀ṣẹ́ fi adùn kun ara; ìlera tí ó kún fún ayọ̀ ni ẹ̀bùn tí ó ga jùlọ. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ stripped away sickness, and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ poured sweetness over the body; health crowned with joy is the supreme gift: Wholeness restores radiance.)

Oyin kì í korò lẹ́nu ẹni tí ó ba san; orí rere ló ń sọ àìlera di orin ayọ̀. (Honey is never bitter in the mouth of the healed person; a favored destiny turns weakness into a song of triumph: Healing brings joyous celebration.)
ODU_225_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Ọ̀ṣẹ́.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_226_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òfún.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ìrẹtẹ̀-Fún, the supreme conclusion of the Ìrẹtẹ̀ healing cycle, sealing physical restoration with Ọbàtálá's primordial white clay and pure peace. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by supreme elders to conclude community purification festivals. Contemporary/Diaspora: Maintained in Lucumí as Irete Fun, crowning medical recovery with sacred purity.
ODU_226_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òfún.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ìrẹtẹ̀ (healing action, purification) and Òfún (primordial white chalk, creation, ultimate peace). Teaches that physical healing culminates in spiritual purity; when the body is cleansed and the spirit rests in Ọbàtálá's light, complete wholeness is realized.
ODU_226_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òfún.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/I/II/I on right and II/I/II/I on left. The Babaláwo marks a ring of white chalk (Ẹfun) around Ọpọ́n Ifá. Involves pure white chalk (Ẹfun), Ewé Òdúndún, cold water, sixteen snails, and white cloth.
ODU_226_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òfún.social_and_ritual_context: Cast to celebrate full recovery from life-threatening illness, crowning ancestral shrine purifications, and concluding guild festivals.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ wo ara sàn, Òfún fi ẹfun mímọ́ wọ̀ ọ́; àlàáfíà tí Ọbàtálá fún ni kì í parun. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ healed the body, and Òfún clothed it in sacred white chalk; the serene peace bestowed by Ọbàtálá never perishes: Primordial purity crowns complete recovery.)

Ẹni tí ó ba bọ́ nínú àrùn gbọ́dọ̀ dúpẹ́ lọ́wọ́ Ọlọ́run; ìwà mímọ́ ni odi tí ń dáàbò bo ẹ̀mí. (He who escapes sickness must express gratitude to the Divine; a pure conscience is the rampart that protects human life: Sacred gratitude preserves health.)
ODU_226_Ìrẹtẹ̀_Òfún.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_227_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ogbè.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity (c. 11th–14th Century CE): Codified at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as Ọ̀ṣẹ́-Ogbè, also celebrated as Ọ̀ṣẹ́-Bí-Ogbè, the paramount sovereign chapter of artistic magnificence, melodic eloquence, royal wealth, and visual radiance. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by master bronze casters, beadworkers, and court musicians in Oyo and Benin empires. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Ose Nilogbe / Ose Ogbè, renowned for unyielding prosperity and artistic fame.
ODU_227_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ogbè.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (I/II/I/II: victory, sweetness, artistic radiance, Ọ̀ṣun's grace) on the right and Ogbè (I/I/I/I: primordial light, total triumph) on the left of Ọpọ́n Ifá. Dialectically unites beauty and absolute light, teaching that true civilization reaches its zenith when power is guided by beauty, aesthetic harmony, and moral sweetness.
ODU_227_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ogbè.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn across Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/II/I/II on the right and I/I/I/I on the left. The Babaláwo taps the northern perimeter with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Ajé, Ewé Ọ̀ṣun, pure honey, yellow brass bell, sixteen cowries, and a white pigeon.
ODU_227_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ogbè.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for royal artists, master musicians, bead artisans, merchants seeking commercial prominence, and dedicating new cultural centers.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀ṣẹ́ bí Ogbè sí ayé, gbogbo ilé kún fún ìmọ́lẹ̀ àti ayọ̀; ẹwà tí a fi ọgbọ́n tọ́ kì í rẹ̀wẹ̀sì. (Ọ̀ṣẹ́ birt Ogbè into the world, and every home was filled with radiance and joy; beauty guided by wisdom never fades: Aesthetic harmony illuminated by light commands universal respect.)

Ọrọ̀ tí ń bọ̀ wá kì í kọjú sẹ́yìn; ẹnu tí ó bá ń kọrin ayọ̀ kì í ráhùn ebi. (The prosperity that approaches never turns its back; the voice that sings songs of joy never complains of hunger: Radiant positivity attracts lasting abundance.)
ODU_227_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ogbè.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_228_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀ṣẹ́-Yẹ̀kú, governing the transformation of mourning into celebratory remembrance, funerary poetic chants (Rárà), and honoring departed ancestors through beauty. 19th-Century Era: Consulted during grand funerary ceremonies for paramount rulers. Contemporary/Diaspora: Preserved in Lucumí as Ose Yeku, invoked for ancestral appeasement through artistic offerings.
ODU_228_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (beauty, sweetness, song) and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (ancestral twilight, mortality, cooling). Teaches that death cannot extinguish the memory of a virtuous life; true art and poetry transform the pain of bereavement into enduring ancestral celebration.
ODU_228_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá with Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/II/I/II on right and II/II/II/II on left. The Babaláwo uses an Ìrọ́kẹ́ to direct offerings toward the southern realm. Involves Ewé Ìran, Ewé Akòko, dark earthenware vessel, honey, and a black hen.
ODU_228_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.social_and_ritual_context: Divined during funeral commemorations, ancestral shrine dedications, and transforming family sorrow into celebratory unity.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀ṣẹ́ kọrin ayọ̀ sí ojú Ọ̀yẹ̀kú, ó sọ ìbànújẹ́ di orin; ikú kì í pa orúkọ ẹni rere rẹ́. (Ọ̀ṣẹ́ sang joyful melodies before Ọ̀yẹ̀kú, transforming grief into song; death never erases the name of the righteous: Noble memory outlives mortality.)

Bí ewé bá bọ́ lára igi, ilẹ̀ ló ń padà sí; orísun tí kò gbàgbé kì í gbẹ. (When the leaf falls from the bough, it returns to the nourishing earth; the spring that is never forgotten never dries: Filial remembrance sustains lineage immortality.)
ODU_228_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art.

ODU_229_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìwòrì.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀ṣẹ́-Wòrì, governing creative vision in brass-casting and wood-carving guilds, inspired dreaming, and aesthetic contemplation. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by master sculptors crafting royal veranda posts and doors in Oyo and Ekiti. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Ose Paure / Ose Iwori, celebrated for creative intuition.
ODU_229_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìwòrì.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (aesthetic beauty, artistic sweetness) and Ìwòrì (visionary perception, deep contemplation). Emphasizes that genuine masterpieces emerge when technical skill is guided by deep spiritual insight; superficial art lacks the soul that commands reverence.
ODU_229_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìwòrì.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/II/I/II on right and II/I/I/II on left. The Babaláwo strikes the upper right rim with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Gbégbé, Ewé Àjídèwe, brass filings, honey, and a white pigeon.
ODU_229_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìwòrì.social_and_ritual_context: Cast for sculptors, architects, poets, and textile weavers beginning major royal commissions.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìwòrì wo àwòrán ní inú ọkàn, Ọ̀ṣẹ́ gbẹ́ ẹ jáde ní ẹwà; ọgbọ́n inú ló ń sọ igi di adé. (Ìwòrì beheld the vision in the soul, and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ carved it forth in beauty; inner wisdom transforms plain timber into a crown: Inspired vision elevates material craftsmanship.)

Ẹwà tí kò ní ìmọ̀ jinlẹ̀ kò lè tọ́jọ́; orísun ọgbọ́n ló ń gbé iṣẹ́ ọnà ga. (Beauty devoid of deep contemplation cannot endure; the spring of wisdom elevates true art: Spiritual depth immortalizes artistic creation.)
ODU_229_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìwòrì.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle.

ODU_230_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Òdí.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀ṣẹ́-Dí, governing the protection of matrimonial intimacy, safeguarding reproductive fertility against envious sabotage, and fortifying beauty with moral boundaries. 19th-Century Era: Consulted during royal weddings to shield the new union from palace rivalries. Contemporary/Diaspora: Maintained in Lucumí as Ose Di, renowned for protecting relationships.
ODU_230_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Òdí.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (beauty, sweetness, matrimonial joy) and Òdí (rampart, closure, protective foundation). Teaches that radiant love and domestic beauty must be sheltered behind firm moral boundaries; exposing intimate vulnerability to public malice invites destruction.
ODU_230_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Òdí.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/II/I/II on right and I/II/II/I on left. The Babaláwo seals the mark with a smooth river pebble. Involves Ewé Pèrègún, Ewé Ọ̀ṣun, river stone, pure honey, and a white dove.
ODU_230_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Òdí.social_and_ritual_context: Divined for newlyweds, protecting pregnancies from hostile relatives, and guarding valuable artistic assets from theft.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀ṣẹ́ kọ́ ilé ẹwà, Òdí mọ odi mọ́ ọn; ifẹ́ tí ó fi sùúrù kọ́ odi kì í wó. (Ọ̀ṣẹ́ built the pavilion of beauty, and Òdí erected a rampart around it; love that patiently builds defensive walls never collapses: Moral boundaries protect domestic bliss.)

A kì í fi ohun ìní tí ó dára hàn olè; ààbò tòótọ́ ló ń pa ayọ̀ mọ́. (One does not display precious treasures before thieves; genuine discretion preserves enduring joy: Prudent secrecy safeguards beauty.)
ODU_230_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Òdí.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.

ODU_231_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìrosùn.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀ṣẹ́-Rosùn, governing royal cosmetic adornment, the red camwood (Osùn) rituals of maidenhood, and celebrating ancestral grace in communal dances. 19th-Century Era: Consulted during the annual harvest and maiden initiation ceremonies. Contemporary/Diaspora: Retained in Lucumí as Ose Leso / Ose Iroso, celebrated for elegance and honor.
ODU_231_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìrosùn.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (beauty, adornment) and Ìrosùn (ancestral blood, camwood, vigilance). Teaches that true beauty is not superficial vanity, but an outward embodiment of ancestral virtue, dignity, and wholesome character (*Ìwà Pẹ̀lẹ́*).
ODU_231_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìrosùn.material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I/II/I/II on right and I/I/II/II on left. The Babaláwo blends pure camwood with Ìyẹ̀rosùn across Ọpọ́n Ifá. Involves Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, Osùn powder, white rooster, pure honey, and red beads.
ODU_231_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìrosùn.social_and_ritual_context: Cast during bridal cosmetic preparations, dedication of sacred dance ensembles, and public festivals honoring ancestral maidens.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀ṣẹ́ kun osùn sí ara, Ìrosùn tẹ adé ọ̀wọ̀ lé e lórí; ẹwà tí ó ní ìwà rere ni adé ayé. (Ọ̀ṣẹ́ anointed the body with camwood, and Ìrosùn placed the crown of honor upon it; beauty accompanied by virtuous character is the crown of life: Moral integrity crowns visual elegance.)

Osùn kì í parẹ́ lára àwọn tí ń jó; orí rere ló ń mú kí iṣẹ́ ọnà tàn mọ́lẹ̀. (Camwood never vanishes from the dancing initiates; a favored destiny makes artistic skill shine brightly: Graceful conduct enhances honor.)
ODU_231_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ìrosùn.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Drewal, H.J. & Pemberton, J. (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art.

ODU_232_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀ṣẹ́-Wọ́nrín, governing the resolution of sudden domestic disputes through musical performance, diplomatic gifts, and calming unforeseen turbulence with festive generosity. 19th-Century Era: Consulted by village peace emissaries navigating regional border disputes. Contemporary/Diaspora: Preserved in Lucumí as Ose Ojuani, invoked for averting sudden misfortune through generosity.
ODU_232_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (sweetness, beauty, joy) and Ọ̀wọ́nrín (sudden reversal, stormy change). Teaches that unexpected conflicts and volatile domestic crises are disarmed through sweet diplomacy and generous celebration; responding to fury with venom only feeds the tempest.
ODU_232_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.material_and_craftsmanship: Marked upon Ọpọ́n Ifá as I/II/I/II on right and II/II/I/I on left. The Babaláwo strikes the southwestern edge with an ivory Ìrọ́kẹ́. Involves Ewé Iná, Ewé Ọ̀dúndún, pure honey, roasted corn, palm oil, and a spotted hen.
ODU_232_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.social_and_ritual_context: Divined during sudden domestic arguments, business partnership frictions, and sudden financial swings requiring reconciliatory diplomacy.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀wọ́nrín fẹ́ afẹ́fẹ́ sí ilé, Ọ̀ṣẹ́ da oyin sí i; ọ̀rọ̀ sùúrù ló ń pa iná ìjà. (Ọ̀wọ́nrín blew a gale into the home, and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ poured honey upon it; patient speech quenches the fires of contention: Gentle diplomacy neutralizes sudden discord.)

Bí ìjà bá dé, a kì í fi ibi gbèjà; ẹ̀bùn àlàáfíà ló ń mú ìṣẹ́gun wá. (When strife arrives, one does not defend oneself with wickedness; the gift of peace brings enduring victory: Generous resolution outlasts hostility.)
ODU_232_Ọ̀ṣẹ́_Ọ̀wọ́nrín.provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé.
